## Outline

1. **The measurement problem** — one task shared by the suspensions and calibration groups, and the cost of present practice.
2. **The estimator** — periodic multisine, leakage-free synchronous DFT, measured per-bin covariance, maximum-likelihood fit, Cramér–Rao bound.
3. **The measurement in the time domain** — record length, drive headroom, and identification with the loops closed.
4. **Suspensions** — HSTS and SRM through production damping banks, and the 40m SOS in 6 DOF.
5. **Calibration** — `R(f)`, the per-stage `κᵢ`, and drift tracking.
6. **Outlook** — the staged plan, and the operational answers needed from the control room.

::: {.notes}
Pacing: sections 1–3 are the shared method argument, followed by a Suspensions
block, a Calibration block, and the request at the end. For a 25-minute slot,
give one group its own block and cover the other's in two slides.

Set expectations here: everything shown is Phase 1 — the RTSfreerun digital twin
running the same compiled advligorts front-end C code as a real front end. There
are no hardware injections anywhere in this deck. The final section sets out what
would be needed in order to go further.
:::

## Two groups, one measurement problem

::: {.aud-sus}
**Suspensions** — `f₀`, `Q`, and the cross-couplings of the rigid-body modes,
measured through the damping loops as they are normally run, without committing a
shift to it.
:::

::: {.aud-cal}
**Calibration** — `R(f)`, the actuation strengths `κᵢ`, and their drift, with
defensible uncertainties.
:::

Both are the same task: to measure a transfer function accurately under a fixed
drive budget and a fixed measurement time.

This talk covers what the Pintelon–Schoukens method offers relative to swept sine
and broadband noise, and what it currently achieves on the compiled CDS digital
twin.

## Rigid-body modes over the readout floor

![](figs/problem.svg){.r-stretch}

Sharp, high-`Q` rigid-body modes packed into a few Hz, over a readout floor.
Nearly all the information about `f₀` and `Q` lives in a handful of bins per mode.

::: {.notes}
The point of this slide is that the information is localised. Any drive that
spreads power uniformly across the band spends most of its budget where the
parameters are not.
:::

## Present practice and its costs

| practice | what it costs |
|---|---|
| Swept sine — one line at a time, dwell, step | correct, but pays wall-clock linearly in the number of frequencies |
| Broadband noise with Welch estimation | the record is not periodic, so the DFT leaks; a high-`Q` peak is read low, and the bias does not average away |
| Ad-hoc drive shaping | no per-bin noise model, so no defensible error bar and no stopping rule |

None of these is incorrect. Each leaves information, and measurement time, unused.

## The Pintelon–Schoukens estimator

1. Design a periodic multisine whose power is placed according to the Fisher information.
2. Inject it for an integer number of periods and discard the transient period or periods.
3. Estimate the FRF by a synchronous DFT — the drive period equals the analysis
   window, so the estimate is leakage-free — as a ratio of averages `⟨Y⟩/⟨X⟩`, with
   the per-bin noise covariance obtained from the period-to-period scatter.
4. Fit the parametric model by maximum likelihood using that covariance.
5. Bound the result by the Cramér–Rao bound from the accumulated Fisher
   information, and return that bound to step 1.

The iteration terminates when the fractional parameter uncertainty `σ/θ` reaches
its target.

::: {.notes}
Step 3 carries most of the weight: periodicity is what makes the noise model
measured rather than assumed. Steps 1 and 5 make the measurement a design problem
rather than a post-processing problem.
:::

## The three drives, side by side

![](figs/excitations.svg){.r-stretch}

Same in-band power. Only the multisine is exactly periodic in the analysis
window.

::: {.notes}
Crest factors printed here are plant-referred — peak/RMS of the requested drive.
The binding actuator limit is DAC saturation after the whitening/actuation
chain, which this simulation does not model, so no peak/crest advantage is being
claimed for any phasing choice.
:::

# The measurement in the time domain {.divider}

## The injected drive

![](figs/td-drive.svg){.r-stretch}

{{< var td.n_periods >}} identical periods of {{< var td.period >}} s
(`df = {{< var td.df >}} Hz`), ramped on and off with a Tukey window so nothing
is stepped into the suspension. The peak sits at {{< var td.peak_frac >}}% of the
{{< var td.dac >}}-count coil-driver limit.

::: {.notes}
The ramp is functional rather than cosmetic: an abrupt start excites the full
band and then requires waiting for the ringdown. The ramp is excluded from the
analysis window; only whole periods in steady state are transformed.
:::

## Period-to-period repeatability

![](figs/td-periods.svg){.r-stretch}

Overlaying the steady-state periods, they agree to better than 1 part in
10^{{< var td.spread_pow >}}^ of full scale, which is machine precision. That is
the basis for the leakage-free DFT: an integer number of periods in the window
means every excited tone lands exactly on a bin.

The first {{< var td.skip >}} periods are discarded. The transient is visible on
the right panel and is what a non-periodic estimator would smear into the
spectrum.

::: {.notes}
This is the time-domain counterpart of the leakage slide, and the evidence for
the leakage-free claim: the record repeats, so the DFT of one period and the DFT
of the whole record agree bin for bin.
:::

## Ringdown sets the record length

![](figs/td-ringdown.svg){.r-stretch}

Undamped, the {{< var td.tau_open >}} s decay is what forces `T ≳ Q/f₀`. With the
local dampers engaged the same mode decays in {{< var td.tau_damped >}} s, so
steady state is reached in seconds rather than minutes.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Damping is often treated as an obstacle to the measurement. Here it shortens the
required record, and the reference-based FRF cancels the controller in any case,
so the optic need not be undamped in order to be identified.
:::

## Drive headroom: spectrum shape and phasing

![](figs/td-headroom.svg){.r-stretch}

Both drives carry the same power at the same (Schroeder) phasing. The crest
factor is {{< var td.crest_opt >}} for the optimal drive and
{{< var td.crest_flat >}} for the flat one, so concentrating the power onto the
modes carries no penalty in peak.

The advantage of the optimal drive comes from placing that identical power where
the parameters are informative, not from a different peak-to-RMS ratio.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Peak here is plant-referred. The limit that binds is at the DAC, downstream of
the whitening chain — see the future-work slide.
:::

::: {.notes}
Be precise about what this figure shows: both drives use the same Schroeder
phasing, so this is a spectrum-shape comparison, not a phase comparison — it
says concentrating power costs no peak. It matches the tutorial's Schroeder row
(1.84 flat / 1.93 concentrated) independently.

The separate question of whether the phase choice recovers headroom is addressed
in the tutorial and on the planned-work slide, not here: crest factor is not
invariant under filtering, and the binding limit sits at the DAC, downstream of
the whitening chain.
:::

## Drive and response

![](figs/td-response.svg){.r-stretch}

A bounded, periodic, ramped drive and the corresponding periodic response. The
excitation stays well within the actuator range throughout.

## Periodicity, leakage, and the measured noise model

![](figs/leakage.svg){.r-stretch}

A `Q = {{< var leak.Q >}}` mode at equal power over {{< var leak.T >}} s; the
linewidth spans {{< var leak.bins >}} bins.

- multisine peak bias {{< var leak.ms_bias >}}%; windowed-random peak bias {{< var leak.w_bias >}}%
- combined at the peak, the random estimator is {{< var leak.rmse_ratio >}}× worse in RMSE over {{< var leak.seeds >}} seeds

::: {.notes}
The Welch estimate is both biased and noisier. The bias is the consequential
part: additional averaging does not remove it, so a windowed random measurement
of a high-Q mode systematically under-reports the peak, and therefore the Q.
:::

## Band coverage per unit time

![](figs/swept.svg){.r-stretch}

One multisine window ({{< var sweep.T >}} s) measures {{< var sweep.bins >}} bins.
In the same wall-clock a sweep reaches {{< var sweep.pts >}} points; covering the
same band to the same per-bin σ requires approximately
{{< var sweep.cover_h >}} h, which is {{< var sweep.factor >}}× the single
multisine window.

## Fisher information and drive allocation

For a model `H(f, θ)` measured at lines `fₖ` with drive PSD `Pxx(fₖ)` and noise
`Pyy(fₖ)`, the Fisher information is

$$
\mathcal{I}(\theta) \;=\; 2T \sum_k \frac{P_{xx}(f_k)}{P_{yy}(f_k)}\,
\mathrm{Re}\!\left[\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta}^{\!H}\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta}\right]_{f_k}
$$

and the attainable covariance is `𝓘⁻¹`, the Cramér–Rao bound.

- The information scales as the square of the drive amplitude, so the drive level
  is a design variable rather than a constraint.
- The optimal `Pxx` is not flat. P&S solve it by the dispersion-function fixed
  point under a fixed power budget, and power concentrates at the modes.
- The first pass is prior-robust: the design is averaged over `f₀·[1±u]`, so an
  inaccurate prior remains covered.

## The designed drive

![](figs/optimal-design.svg){.r-stretch}

Gold denotes the Fisher-optimal multisine; grey denotes an equal-power flat drive,
included as a baseline and not as the injected waveform. The CRB variance-reduction
factor at equal power and record length is F = {{< var head.F >}}.

::: {.notes}
F is computed from fisher.parameter_covariance, not fitted: it is the ratio of the
worst-diagonal CRB variance between the flat and the optimal design at identical
power and record length.
:::

## Uncertainty at fixed drive, drive at fixed uncertainty

![](figs/convergence.svg){.r-stretch}

- the optimal design at power `P` reaches `σ/θ ≤ {{< var head.target >}}` in
  {{< var head.ttt_opt >}} passes ({{< var head.t_pass >}} s each); the flat design
  does not reach it within the same budget
- reduced to `P/{{< var head.F >}}`, the optimal drive matches the flat design's σ
  at {{< var head.rms_drop >}}× less in-band drive

The second case is the one of operational interest: the same parameter
uncertainty at reduced force on the optic.

## Calibration of the quoted uncertainty

![](figs/crb-pull.svg){.r-stretch}

Over {{< var pull.seeds >}} independent measurements, the normalised errors
`(fit − true)/σ_CRB` are consistent with 𝒩(0,1): empirical σ = {{< var pull.std >}},
mean {{< var pull.mean >}}.

The maximum-likelihood fit attains the bound, so the quoted uncertainty is the
realised one.

::: {.notes}
This result underlies every uncertainty quoted subsequently. Were the pulls not
of unit width, the CRB would carry no operational meaning.
:::

## Identification with the loops closed

![](figs/closed-loop.svg){.r-stretch}

Driving after the controller and reading the drive monitor `u`, the
reference-based FRF `⟨Y⟩/⟨U⟩` returns the open-loop plant through a loop
suppressing the resonance {{< var cl.supp >}}×, recovered to
{{< var cl.rel >}}%. The naive FRF against the injected reference returns the
suppressed response.

::: {.notes}
This is why the suspensions results later can be taken with the production damping
loops closed. The controller cancels in the ratio, provided the actual plant input
is measured rather than the requested reference.
:::

# Suspensions {.divider}

## The test stand: a compiled CDS front end

Phase 1 runs against the RTSfreerun digital twin — an advligorts model compiled
from its `.mdl` and driven in-process, so identification runs against the same C
numerics a real front end runs:

- `x1hsts` — HSTS drive→sensor cascade, order 10, 5 modes 0.67–3.78 Hz, `Q ≈ 50`
- `x1hsts6dof` — bare-M1 6×6 HSTS state-space plant and per-DOF `cdsFilt`
  dampers, loaded with production foton banks (L1-MC2 / L1-SRM) and the
  engaged-FM list from the archived L1 SDF
- the twin's own `ligo-india` seismic and BOSEM readout-noise presets as the background

Everything below is measured through that stack, with no hardware.

::: {.notes}
Worth stressing: the filter banks are the site's, not ours; the plant comes from
aligo-suspension-models; the noise levels are the twin's presets. The only thing
supplied here is the excitation and the estimator.
:::

## Through the real damping loops

With all six production L1-MC2 top-mass dampers closed on `x1hsts6dof`
(`df = {{< var loops.df_hz >}} Hz`, {{< var loops.n_periods >}} periods,
{{< var loops.n_passes >}} passes, measured for this talk):

- the reference-based FRF recovers the open-loop diagonal on all six DOF, worst
  {{< var loops.closed_max >}}%, median {{< var loops.closed_med >}}%, pitch and
  yaw included
- with the loops open, the same tensor scores worst {{< var loops.open_max >}}%,
  median {{< var loops.open_med >}}%
- the physical `L↔P` and `R↔Y` cross-couplings are recovered at
  {{< var loops.coup_min >}}–{{< var loops.coup_max >}}%

The damper output carries {{< var loops.fb_rms >}}× the injected drive in RMS, so
the loop is active rather than idling.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
An earlier result was nearly reported as a limitation of the method: closed-loop
peaks were 50–110 % in error, which resembled ill-conditioning at the damped
modes. The cause was a sign error in the plant-input reconstruction — the
composite's junction is a `"+−"` sum. The wrong sign is negligible off resonance
and dominates where the loop gain is largest. When several methods fail
identically at the resonances, a shared reconstruction error is the more likely
explanation than a limitation of the estimator.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every number on this slide was measured by `talks/make_figs.py loops` against the
compiled model, with the same knobs as `tests/test_rtsfreerun_6dof.py` — so the
talk and the test assert on the same measurement. An earlier draft quoted
"< 0.1 %" from a recorded campaign; re-measuring gives 0.15 % closed and 0.34 %
open, and couplings up to 1.5 %. The tests only ever asserted < 1 % and < 2 %, so
quote these numbers, not the old ones.
:::

## The 6×6 tensor, open and closed

![](figs/loops-tensor.svg){.r-stretch}

Median relative error per element against the analytic state-space oracle. The
diagonal is the plant; the bright off-diagonal cells are the physical `L↔P` and
`R↔Y` couplings, which are recovered rather than assumed to be zero.

::: {.notes}
Colour is log₁₀ of percent error. Off-diagonals that are structurally near zero
score poorly in relative terms — that is expected and is why the claim is made
on the diagonal and on the two physically dominant couplings, not on all 36.
:::

## The sign error in the plant-input reconstruction

![](figs/td-junction.svg){.r-stretch}

The composite's `COIL_DRV_SUM` is a `"+−"` junction, so the true plant input is
the drive minus the damper feedback. With the loops closed, that feedback term is
not small.

::: {.notes}
This is the time-domain picture of the bug. Off resonance the middle trace is
tiny and the sign cannot matter. At the damped modes it is comparable to the
drive, so the wrong sign corrupts exactly the modes being identified — which is
why the failure looked like an ill-conditioning wall at the resonances.
:::

## Cancellation of the controller

![](figs/td-cancellation.svg){.r-stretch}

The same closed-loop data, formed two ways. Dividing by the injected drive
returns the suppressed closed-loop response, down {{< var loops.naive_supp >}}×
at the peak with {{< var loops.naive_bias >}}% median error. Dividing by the
reconstructed plant input returns the open-loop plant to
{{< var loops.ref_bias >}}%.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The damping loops need not be disengaged for the identification. The FRF must be
formed against the reconstructed plant input rather than against the injected
reference.
:::

## SRM: a joint modal fit through production dampers

The SRM is an HSTS identified through its production L1-SRM damping banks, all six
loops closed, under the twin's full seismic and OSEM background.

- one prior-robust multisine per actuator, `df = {{< var srm.df_hz >}} Hz`
  ({{< var srm.period >}} s per period), 16 periods, giving `dof = {{< var srm.dof >}}`
- the open-loop diagonal FRF is recovered to {{< var srm.diag >}}% median against
  the analytic state-space oracle, with the controllers engaged
- a rank-1 joint modal fit: shared poles across all 6×6 elements, with the order
  chosen blind from the data (peak union, prominence-gated) and the oracle used
  only to score

{{< var srm.n_good >}} of {{< var srm.n_modes >}} modes are recovered well in both
`f₀` and `Q`; the median `|Δf₀|` is {{< var srm.df_med >}}% and the median `Q`
error {{< var srm.q_med >}}% across the {{< var srm.n_wellsep >}} well-separated
modes.

::: {.notes}
One caveat to state if asked: the OSEM readout noise is injected at the
damper's sensor node rather than through an in-loop quantised sensor — the compiled
model cannot splice a sensor between plant and damper without a rebuild. The
seismic and OSEM disturbances are genuinely in-loop; the sensor quantisation is
not modelled. Seismic is referred to M1 displacement through the real gnd→M1
residues and the ISI transmissibility, then divided by the plant and injected at
the coil-drive node, so the motion the damper acts against is the correct in-loop
motion.
:::

## One diagonal element, through the resonances

![](figs/srm-diag.svg){.r-stretch}

The per-bin nonparametric inverse scatters at the peaks; the parametric fit passes
through them, since it fits a model rather than reading a spectrum.

## The 0.672 / 0.676 Hz doublet is spatial

![](figs/srm-doublet.svg){.r-stretch}

Δf₀ ≈ {{< var srm.doublet_mhz >}} mHz, well inside one linewidth
(`Γ = f₀/Q ≈ 13 mHz`). It is not a resolution problem: the plant
block-diagonalises into the orthogonal `{L,P,V}` and `{T,R,Y}` planes
(cross-coupling ~1e-13). Fitting each plane alone resolves both members.

## Consequences for the fit parameterization

| fit | `f₀` recovered |
|---|---|
| shared-pole 6×6 | one blended pole — the pair is collapsed |
| block-decoupled, L–P–V plane | {{< var srm.plane0_f0 >}} Hz ± {{< var srm.plane0_f0_sigma >}}, Q = {{< var srm.plane0_Q >}} |
| block-decoupled, T–R–Y plane | {{< var srm.plane1_f0 >}} Hz ± {{< var srm.plane1_f0_sigma >}}, Q = {{< var srm.plane1_Q >}} |

No finer `df`, no super-resolution and no doublet-concentrated drive were
required. The apparent non-identifiability followed from the parameterization —
a single shared pole set imposed across two orthogonal modes.

::: {.notes}
The general point: compute the bound before describing something as unresolvable.
Parametric maximum likelihood super-resolves — two modes separated by Δf with
linewidth Γ are resolvable once SNR·N ≳ (Γ/Δf)⁴, which is finite and reachable by
increasing SNR or record length. The non-parametric Rayleigh limit does not apply
to a parametric fit. In this case even that was unnecessary: the pair is
separated spatially rather than spectrally.
:::

## The 40m SOS in 6 DOF, against the bound

![](figs/sos-crb.svg){.r-stretch}

{{< var sos.n_modes >}} rigid-body modes of a single-stage 40m SOS, identified as a
6-DOF MIMO system. The worst pull is {{< var sos.worst_sigma >}}σ and the worst
`f₀` error {{< var sos.worst_f0_pct >}}%.

::: {.notes}
Read the Q panel with the bound in mind, and say so out loud: the pulls are all
inside ~1.6σ, but the σ's differ a lot between modes. The side (T) mode's Q has a
wide CRB because this low-band design spends most of its lines on L and P; its
recovered Q is consistent with truth, just loosely bounded. Tightening it is a
line-placement and record-length choice — more lines on the T linewidth, longer T
— not a limit. That is what the CRB is for: it identifies where to spend the next
measurement.
:::

## How that campaign was designed

The excitation design determines the result:

- two focused campaigns rather than one sweep. The low band `0.4–1.2 Hz` drives
  `L,P,T,Y`; the high band `14–26 Hz` drives `V,R`. A single broadband pass
  collapses the per-bin covariance to rank 1 off-resonance and the `{L,P}`
  whitening goes singular.
- lines clustered on the modes: 25 lines per mode spanning ±8 linewidths, plus
  a few off-resonance anchors for the baseline.
- a block-decoupled fit — only `L–P` is coupled; the `L/T` pair is 1.8 mHz apart
  and is scored per-DOF so a nearest-frequency match cannot silently swap them.
- the plant is built with python-control from the 40m physical parameters and
  gated on the measured modes (pend 1, pitch 0.6, yaw 0.7, side 1, vert 16,
  roll 16√2 Hz); side is not fitted and lands −0.18 % from 1 Hz.

::: {.notes}
The rank-deficiency point is the transferable one. Driving flat and then whitening
with the measured covariance leaves the off-resonance bins uninformative and the
whitening singular. Clustering the lines is what keeps the estimator conditioned.
:::

# Calibration {.divider}

## The DARM twin

The Phase-1 DARM twin: sensing `C` (cavity pole and delay), three-stage actuation
`κ_UIM / κ_PUM / κ_TST`, the derived servo `D`, and the response

$$ R(f) \;=\; \frac{1 + G(f)}{C(f)}, \qquad G = C\,D\,A $$

Pcal serves as the absolute reference: forming `H_stage / H_pcal` cancels the
sensing function, so the actuation strengths are recovered independently of
sensing drift.

The pipeline is unchanged: periodic multisine, leakage-free reference FRF with a
measured per-bin covariance, maximum-likelihood fit, Cramér–Rao bound.

Sensing: cavity pole {{< var darm.fcc_fit >}} ± {{< var darm.fcc_sigma >}} Hz
(true {{< var darm.fcc >}}); delay {{< var darm.tau_fit >}} ± {{< var darm.tau_sigma >}} µs
(true {{< var darm.tau >}}).

| stage | true `κ` | recovered ± σ(CRB) | error | pull |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| UIM | {{< var darm.k_uim_true >}} | {{< var darm.k_uim >}} ± {{< var darm.k_uim_sigma >}} | {{< var darm.k_uim_pct >}}% | {{< var darm.k_uim_pull >}}σ |
| PUM | {{< var darm.k_pum_true >}} | {{< var darm.k_pum >}} ± {{< var darm.k_pum_sigma >}} | {{< var darm.k_pum_pct >}}% | {{< var darm.k_pum_pull >}}σ |
| TST | {{< var darm.k_tst_true >}} | {{< var darm.k_tst >}} ± {{< var darm.k_tst_sigma >}} | {{< var darm.k_tst_pct >}}% | {{< var darm.k_tst_pull >}}σ |

::: {.notes}
One seed and one record — the pulls are near 2σ on UIM/PUM, which is not a bias
claim. The TST bound is the loosest because that stage has the least authority in
this band; that is the stage the next design should address, and the bound
identifies it before the measurement time is spent.
:::

## A drifting actuation strength `κ(t)`

![](figs/darm-drift.svg){.r-stretch}

A {{< var darm.drift_amp >}} %/hour drift on the TST stage, over
{{< var darm.span_min >}} minutes, sampled by {{< var darm.n_snap >}} leakage-free
snapshots. The plant drifts on a timescale far longer than one record, so each
record is locally stationary.

## Tracking residual against the bound

![](figs/darm-tracking.svg){.r-stretch}

`κ(t) = Σ cₖ bₖ(t)` in a Legendre time basis — a Lataire–Pintelon basis expansion
in two-step form. The coefficient covariance `(BᵀWB)⁻¹` is the Cramér–Rao bound on
`κ(t)` and `κ̇(t)`.

## Joint recovery of several drifting parameters

![](figs/darm-joint.svg){.r-stretch}

Optical gain, SRC detuning and a stage `κ` drifting together under a correlated
random walk, recovered jointly, each within its own CRB band. The correlation
matrix of the joint fit indicates which drifts are separable.

## Fisher-optimal placement of the calibration lines

![](figs/darm-callines.svg){.r-stretch}

A-optimal calibration lines placed where the joint drift estimate is sharpest.
The same Fisher argument used for the suspension campaigns applies to continuous
TDCF lines as to a one-shot sweep.

## Resolvability of the drift

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| injected drift amplitude | {{< var darm.drift_amp >}}% of `κ` |
| per-snapshot σ_κ | {{< var darm.snap_sigma >}}% of `κ` |
| tracking σ_κ (LP fit) | {{< var darm.track_sigma >}}% of `κ` |
| ratio of amplitude to tracking σ | {{< var darm.resolve >}}× |
| local-stationarity error (record ÷ drift timescale) | {{< var darm.local_stat >}}% |

The drift is resolved by a computed factor rather than by inspection. We do not
describe a result as limited without first computing the bound that would
establish the limit.

::: {.notes}
Roadmap from here, in order: realistic GP/correlated drift instead of a
deterministic profile; the SRC-detuning optical spring parameterized on the
physical detuning φ(t) so the DARM pole migrates real→complex; several parameters
drifting jointly; the one-shot Lataire–Pintelon fit; continuous TDCF lines; then
the actuation/DAC chain.
:::

## Planned work {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Suspensions**

- **Foton drop-in.** Return the fit as a ZPK/SOS foton bank with a provenance
  manifest — drive used, record length, per-parameter σ, date — so a damping
  redesign starts from a measured plant rather than a model.
- **Q and f₀ trending.** The same campaign run monthly becomes a health
  monitor: a rubbing magnet, a drifting blade spring or a changed cross-coupling
  appears as a parameter moving outside its own CRB.
- **Per-OSEM identification.** Identify in the OSEM basis rather than Euler to
  catch a single weak or stuck coil. At present `V` and `R` have no OSEM
  actuation at all — rank 4 of 6.
- **Track B joint MIMO fit.** Shared poles across all 36 elements rather than
  per-element fits, so cross-couplings and modes are estimated together.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Calibration**

- **κ(t) between full sweeps.** Track the slow parameters continuously from the
  permanent lines and reserve the full campaign for when the tracker indicates
  the model has moved, reducing calibration downtime.
- **A-optimal line allocation.** Choose calibration-line frequencies and
  amplitudes from the Fisher matrix for the reported parameters, under the
  available actuator budget.
- **Hierarchical hand-off with propagated uncertainties.** Propagate the CRB
  through the TST/PUM/UIM crossovers rather than stitching separately-fit stages.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Present this as a set of candidates rather than commitments. The two items most
likely to be of immediate use to a working group are the foton drop-in with a
provenance manifest and the Q/f₀ trending; both are modest additions to what
already runs, and both address questions that are actually asked. Everything on
this slide is Phase 1 work on the twin and assumes no hardware access.

If someone pushes back with "but Schroeder phasing minimises the crest factor,
so you get more power under a saturation limit" — that is measured, published,
and answered in the tutorial (§2.1 of "Why optimal excitation"):

- Schroeder IS lower-crest in plant-referred units: 1.84 vs 3.63 ± 0.31 on a flat
  628-bin drive (1.97×). But on the concentrated ~26-line optimal ASD we actually
  use, it is 1.93 vs 2.65 ± 0.27 — only 1.37×, not an order of magnitude.
- Phase does not change the measurement at all. Same plant, same PSD, same seeds:
  FRF error 14.37 % vs 14.49 %, per-bin σ identical to three figures, and the same
  CRB — the CRB does not take phase as an argument, only the line PSD.
- The crest gap is plant-referred, and crest is not invariant under filtering. The
  binding limit is at the DAC, downstream of the whitening chain, and our sim does
  not model that chain — so it cannot even represent the frame where the
  constraint lives.

So the honest position is: phase is not load-bearing here, random is as good as
Schroeder, and a real peak-drive claim requires doing the optimisation in the DAC
frame. That is exactly the future-work item on this slide.
:::

## The drive optimisation we consider most important

Common to both tracks: a DAC-frame, filter-aware drive optimisation. The drive is
presently designed in plant force units, whereas the binding limit is at the DAC,
with whitening and actuation filters in between. Crest factor is not invariant
under filtering, so the phases arranged at synthesis are no longer those seen at
the limiting stage. This is the reason the pipeline claims no peak-drive advantage
from phasing. Carrying the optimisation through the modelled whitening chain would
make such a claim supportable and would recover usable headroom.

Also outstanding: an ISI / seismic-platform demonstration (sensor correction,
blend filters) and coupled ASC, neither of which is yet exercised; and making the
twin validation reproducible by a third party, which at present requires the
compiled model to be built locally.

## What is needed from the control room

Stage 4 adds three bridge pieces that only the operating groups can specify:

1. **Timing and decoherence** — integer-period synchronous capture and the
   per-period drive-line phase walk. What is the real GPS→period alignment and
   fractional-sample drift between awg and nds2?
2. **Pre-injection saturation check** — the watchdog today is post-hoc, per segment.
   What is wanted is a DAC-frame, filter-aware worst-case-peak check before
   anything is injected. What is the counts↔N calibration and the coil/DAC limit
   on the optic that would be done first?
3. **Operational envelope** — damping on or off; stability margin with a comb near
   the UGF; Guardian / lock-state and abort-on-lock-loss.

Also required, and currently blocking: the exact channel names (`_EXC`, drive
monitor, readback), the OSEM basis matrix, and the current foton bank.

::: {.notes}
Do not guess any of these. Each is an operational fact we do not have, and the
standing rule in this project is to ask rather than to assume. This slide is the
request the talk is built around.
:::

## Reproducing this work

```bash
conda env create -f environment.yml && conda activate sysid
uv pip install -e ".[dev,dashboard,docs]"

# pure-Python twin
system_ident run src/system_ident/configs/twin_demo.yml --twin --yes

# compiled advligorts front end (needs the model built into the env)
system_ident run src/system_ident/configs/rtsfreerun_hsts.yml --rtsfreerun --yes
```

- Docs, tutorial and 13 executed worked examples:
  caltechexperimentalgravity.github.io/system_ident
- Code: github.com/CaltechExperimentalGravity/system_ident
- The pure-Python and DARM pages re-execute anywhere. The compiled-twin pages
  (HSTS, SRM) need the rtsfreerun model built into the env — the published site
  serves their frozen results.

## Summary

- A periodic multisine with a synchronous DFT removes leakage bias and yields a
  measured per-bin noise model, so the quoted uncertainty is the realised one.
- Fisher-based allocation of the drive gives {{< var head.sigma_ratio >}}× smaller
  parameter uncertainty at fixed drive, or equal uncertainty at
  {{< var head.rms_drop >}}× lower drive.
- The maximum-likelihood fit attains the CRB (pull σ = {{< var pull.std >}}), so
  the bound is usable as a stopping rule.
- The damping loops need not be opened: the reference-based FRF recovers the
  open-loop plant through the production dampers ({{< var srm.diag >}}% on SRM).
- Suspensions: {{< var srm.n_good >}}/{{< var srm.n_modes >}} SRM modes in `f₀`
  and `Q`; the 0.67 Hz doublet resolved spatially; the 40m SOS in 6 DOF within
  {{< var sos.worst_sigma >}}σ.
- Calibration: `R(f)` with a measured CRB envelope, and a
  {{< var darm.drift_amp >}} %/h `κ` drift tracked at
  {{< var darm.resolve >}}× resolvability.

Next: the rtsfree SOS composite, then the CDS bridge, which is gated on the
operational answers on the previous slide.

## Backup: working rules behind these numbers

1. **Compute the bound before calling anything a limit.** CRB, SNR, actuator
   headroom, resolution — with numbers, or it is not a limit claim. Three
   "fundamental limits" in this project's history were an implementation bug, an
   under-modelled order, and a sign error.
2. **Parametric ML super-resolves.** Never quote the Rayleigh / one-bin /
   one-linewidth non-parametric limit for a model-based fit.
3. **The measurement design consists of controlled variables, not fixed
   constraints** — drive amplitude up to the actuator limit, `df = 1/T`, line
   placement, model order, and the number of periods.
4. **Use the controls library.** Every state-space, `c2d`, FRF and feedback
   operation is python-control; nothing hand-rolled.
5. **Phase 1 only.** Digital twin until the operational questions are answered.
